A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$ and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $ igcup_n X_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. Then there exist signed measures $
u_a,
u_s$ and a measurable real-valued function $f$ such that
$$
u=
u_a+
u_s,\qquad 
u_a\ll\mu,\qquad 
u_s\perp\mu,\qquad 
u_a(E)=\int_E f\,d\mu$$
for every measurable set $E$. The integral is always defined as an extended real number, and $\int_{X_n}|f|\,d\mu<\infty$ for every $n$.

u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that

Assume AC. If $X$ is a submartingale with $C:=\sup_n\mathbb E[X_n^+]<\infty$, then there is an integrable finite random variable $X_\infty$ such that $X_n\to X_\infty$ almost surely.

almost surely and in $L^1$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

If $\mu(X)<\infty$ and an algebra $\mathcal C$ of subsets of X generates $\mathcal A$, then for every $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C\in\mathcal C$ with $\mu(E\mathbin\triangle C)<\varepsilon$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Define $f_\infty(x,y)=\limsup_n f_n(x,y)$, a jointly measurable extended nonnegative function; for each fixed $x$ it agrees almost everywhere with the finite limit from step 1.1. The conditional-expectation averages $g_n^x$ of the integrable density $f_x$ over $\mathcal P_n$ are defined by $g_n^x(y)=\bar\mu(B)^{-1}\int_B f_x\,d\bar\mu$ on positive-measure cells $B$, and by zero on zero-measure cells. Since $\int f_x\,d\bar\mu\le1$, [F4] gives $g_n^x\to f_x$ almost everywhere: $\mathcal P_n$ generates $\mathcal X$. Cellwise $g_n^x\le f_n(x,\cdot)$ because $\int_B f_x\,d\bar\mu\le K(x,B)$, with both averages zero on null cells. Taking limits proves $f_x\le f_\infty(x,\cdot)$ almost everywhere.

For a cell $B$ at partition level $N$, every $n\ge N$ has $\int_Bf_n(x,y)\bar\mu(dy)\le K(x,B)$, since the positive-measure level-$n$ cells inside $B$ contribute only a sub-sum of the kernel masses of a partition of $B$. Fatou therefore gives $\int_Bf_\infty(x,y)\bar\mu(dy)\le K(x,B)$. By [F8], the left side defines a measure; Fatou at the whole space gives its total mass at most one, so both sides are finite measures. Their sum is a finite measure, and [F6] approximates any measurable set in symmetric difference under that sum; the inequality extends from the generating partition algebra to every measurable set. Choose a singular support $N_x$ with $\bar\mu(N_x)=0$ and $S_x(N_x^c)=0$. Since the left measure has density $f_\infty$ with respect to $\bar\mu$, it assigns zero mass to $N_x$. Applying the inequality to $A\cap N_x^c$ therefore gives $\int_Af_\infty\,d\bar\mu\le\int_Af_x\,d\bar\mu$. Together with step 1.2, this proves $f_\infty=f_x$ almost everywhere.

Since $\bar\mu(dy)=w(y)\mu(dy)$, set $p(x,y)=f_\infty(x,y)w(y)$ and $S(x,A)=K(x,A)-\int_Ap(x,y)\mu(dy)$. Step 2.1 shows sectionwise that $S(x,\cdot)=S_x$, a nonnegative subprobability measure singular to $\mu$. The integral is measurable in $x$ by [F5]; hence $S(\cdot,A)$ is measurable for every $A$, and its sections are countably additive. Thus $S$ is a subprobability kernel and the decomposition holds.

The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

For a probability kernel $P$ on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), a measurable set $C$ is **$(m,\epsilon,\nu)$-small** if $m\ge1$ is an integer, $0<\epsilon\le1$, $\nu$ is a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]), and
$$P^m(x,A)\ge\epsilon\nu(A)\quad(x\in C,\ A\in\mathcal X).$$
The inequality is pointwise in $x$ and holds for every measurable $A$.

A **geometric drift inequality outside $C$** consists of a finite-valued measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,\infty)$, constants $0<\lambda<1$ and $0\le b<\infty$, and
$$PV(x):=\int V(y)P(x,dy)\le\lambda V(x)+b\,1_C(x)\quad(x\in\mathsf X).$$
The terms small set and drift are separate hypotheses; neither definition asserts the existence of the other.

When an invariant probability $\pi$ is specified ([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), an **extended geometric drift certificate finite $\pi$-almost everywhere** allows measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,+\infty]$ with $\pi(V<\infty)=1$ and the same pointwise inequality, interpreted in the nonnegative extended reals. This is a separate convention from the finite-valued drift function above. The geometric theorem treats this certificate on $E=\{V<\infty\}$; the original finite-valued convention gives the corresponding bound on the whole state space.

Let $P$ be $\phi$-irreducible on a countably generated space, with nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$. For each $n\ge1$ there are a jointly measurable $p_n$ and a singular residual kernel $S_n$ such that
$$P^n(x,dy)=p_n(x,y)\phi(dy)+S_n(x,dy),$$
and versions may be chosen so that for every $r,s\ge1$ and every $x,y$,
$$p_{r+s}(x,y)\ge\int p_r(x,z)p_s(z,y)\phi(dz),\qquad p_{r+s}(x,y)\ge\int P^r(x,dz)p_s(z,y).$$
For every $x$, $\sum_{n\ge1}p_n(x,y)>0$ for $\phi$-almost every $y$.

Let $\phi$ be a finite nonzero measure on a countably generated measurable space. For measurable $A,B\subseteq\mathsf X^2$, define $E=\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in A,\ (y,z)\in B\}$. If $\phi^{\otimes3}(E)>0$, then there are measurable $C,D$ with $\phi(C),\phi(D)>0$ and $\gamma>0$ such that
$$\phi(A_1(x)\cap B_2(z))\ge\gamma\quad(x\in C,\ z\in D),$$
where $A_1(x)=\{y:(x,y)\in A\}$ and $B_2(z)=\{y:(y,z)\in B\}$.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The

$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty index set, let $(S_i,\mathcal S_i)_{i\in I}$ be measurable spaces, set $S=\prod_{i\in I}S_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra, and let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $S$. For a nonempty block $B\subseteq I$, write $S_B=\prod_{i\in B}S_i$, $S_{-B}=\prod_{i\in I\setminus B}S_i$, let $p_{-B}:S\to S_{-B}$ be the coordinate projection, and define $\pi_{-B}(D):=\pi(p_{-B}^{-1}(D))$ for measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$.

Products and product sigma-algebras use the empty-product convention in [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: if $B=I$, then $S_{-B}$ is the one-point space $\{()\}$ with its trivial sigma-algebra.

A **proper full conditional kernel** for block $B$ is a supplied probability kernel $K_B:S_{-B}\to S_B$ such that for every product-measurable $C\subseteq S$ and every measurable $D\subseteq S_{-B}$,
$$
\pi\bigl(C\cap p_{-B}^{-1}(D)\bigr)=\int_D K_B(z,C_z)\,\pi_{-B}(dz),\qquad C_z:=\{u\in S_B:\operatorname{splice}_B(z,u)\in C\}.
$$
Here $\operatorname{splice}_B(z,u)$ is the unique state whose coordinates on $I\setminus B$ are $z$ and whose coordinates on $B$ are $u$. This is the event-identity definition of a regular conditional distribution of the block given the retained coordinates, with every kernel section a probability measure at every $z$. It makes no existence claim; the A-page density corollary gives one sufficient case.

**Inputs:** The finite product state space and target law from [[def-gibbs-full-conditional-kernel]], a nonempty block $B$, its supplied proper full conditional kernel $K_B$, and a current state $x\in S$.

**Output:** A new state $x'\in S$ whose retained coordinates equal $x_{-B}$ and whose updated block is sampled from $K_B(x_{-B},\cdot)$.

The transition kernel is
$$P_B(x,C)=\int_{S_B}\mathbf1_C\!\left(\operatorname{splice}_B(x_{-B},u)\right)K_B(x_{-B},du),\qquad C\in\mathcal S.$$
Operationally, retain every coordinate outside $B$, draw $u$ from the full conditional kernel at the retained value, and replace the coordinates in $B$ by $u$. The finite product sigma-algebra makes the splice map measurable; the kernel-integral theorem makes the displayed evaluation measurable in $x$. The well-definedness result is [[lem-gibbs-block-update-is-a-probability-kernel]].

**Inputs:** A common finite-product measurable state space $(S,\mathcal S)$ with target probability $\pi$, an integer $m\ge1$, and for each $j=1,\ldots,m$ a nonempty block $B_j$ with its supplied proper full conditional kernel for $\pi$. Invoke [[alg-gibbs-block-update]] for each block to obtain its exact update kernel $P_j:S\to S$. Select random scan, systematic scan, or both; if random scan is selected, also supply fixed weights $w_j\ge0$ with $\sum_{j=1}^m w_j=1$.

**Admissible conditions:** Every $P_j$ acts on this same $(S,\mathcal S)$ and is an exact block-update kernel for this same target $\pi$. The weights are required only for the random-scan branch; systematic scan takes no weights.

**Outputs:** For each selected mode, its one-update random-scan kernel $P_{\rm rand}:S\to S$ or full-sweep systematic kernel $P_{\rm sweep}:S\to S$; for systematic scan, also the phase-indexed single-update kernels $P_1,\ldots,P_m$.

**Random-scan instructions:** At each update, independently draw $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ with probabilities $w_1,\ldots,w_m$ and apply $P_j$ to the current state. The one-update kernel is
$$P_{\rm rand}(x,A)=\sum_{j=1}^m w_jP_j(x,A).$$
Uniform random scan is the special case $w_j=1/m$.

**Systematic-scan instructions:** Starting from the current state, apply $P_1$, then $P_2$, through $P_m$ in that fixed order; repeat the same order for each subsequent sweep. Return the full-sweep kernel $P_{\rm sweep}=P_1\cdots P_m$. Observing after each single update gives the phase-indexed sequence $P_1,\ldots,P_m,P_1,\ldots$ and is generally time-inhomogeneous; observing only at full-sweep boundaries gives a homogeneous chain with kernel $P_{\rm sweep}$. A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. citations.quote: Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

Let $P$ be a $\phi$-irreducible probability kernel ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]) with invariant probability $\pi$ ([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]). The chain is **aperiodic** if there do not exist an integer $d\ge2$ and pairwise disjoint measurable sets $X_1,\ldots,X_d$ such that $\pi(X_1)>0$ and
$$P(x,X_{i+1})=1\quad(x\in X_i,\ 1\le i<d),\qquad P(x,X_1)=1\quad(x\in X_d).$$
Invariance then gives $\pi(X_i)>0$ for every $i$. The sets need not cover the full state space; the definition rules out any positive-mass cyclic part. Aperiodicity does not itself assert convergence.

For a probability kernel $P$ on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), a measurable set $C$ is **$(m,\epsilon,\nu)$-small** if $m\ge1$ is an integer, $0<\epsilon\le1$, $\nu$ is a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]), and
$$P^m(x,A)\ge\epsilon\nu(A)\quad(x\in C,\ A\in\mathcal X).$$
The inequality is pointwise in $x$ and holds for every measurable $A$.

A **geometric drift inequality outside $C$** consists of a finite-valued measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,\infty)$, constants $0<\lambda<1$ and $0\le b<\infty$, and
$$PV(x):=\int V(y)P(x,dy)\le\lambda V(x)+b\,1_C(x)\quad(x\in\mathsf X).$$
The terms small set and drift are separate hypotheses; neither definition asserts the existence of the other.

When an invariant probability $\pi$ is specified ([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), an **extended geometric drift certificate finite $\pi$-almost everywhere** allows measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,+\infty]$ with $\pi(V<\infty)=1$ and the same pointwise inequality, interpreted in the nonnegative extended reals. This is a separate convention from the finite-valued drift function above. The geometric theorem treats this certificate on $E=\{V<\infty\}$; the original finite-valued convention gives the corresponding bound on the whole state space.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $P$ be countably generated, $\phi$-irreducible and aperiodic with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose a $\phi$-positive small set $C$ and finite-valued $V\ge1$ satisfy $PV\le\lambda V+b1_C$ for $0<\lambda<1$. Then there are $M<\infty$ and $0<r<1$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\rm TV}\le M V(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge0).$$
This is geometric ergodicity with a $V$-weighted bound.

Under the same kernel, $\phi$-positive small-set and drift-constant hypotheses, the result also holds if $V:\mathsf X\to[1,+\infty]$ is measurable and finite $\pi$-almost everywhere, with the drift inequality holding pointwise in the extended sense. Then $E=\{V<\infty\}$ is measurable, absorbing and of full $\pi$-measure, and the displayed bound holds for every $x\in E$. Thus extended certificates give the common geometric rate for $\pi$-almost every start, while globally finite certificates give it for every start.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space

distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in

maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and

measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
